item.title: What is an AI agent with its own computer?
item.description: An AI agent with its own computer keeps working in a cloud workspace after you close your laptop. How it works, the risks, and who offers one, from $9 a month.
item.content:encoded:
Construct gives every AI agent its own computer in the cloud, with files, a browser, a terminal, schedules, memory you can correct, and its own email address, from $9 a month. Most of the big platforms that shipped one this year bundle it into a $20 to $200 subscription tied to their own ecosystem, and Simular's plan with an always-on machine costs $500.

For founders and small teams with recurring work, Construct is the one to start with. It costs the least to get going, keeps every finished file in a workspace your team shares, runs schedules with every device switched off, and does not tie your work to one AI lab.

An AI agent with its own computer is an agent that gets a persistent machine in the cloud: a browser, a terminal, a file system, connected apps, and often its own email address. Because the work runs on that machine instead of your laptop, it keeps going when you close the lid, and a job can run on a schedule at 3am without anyone watching.

Why do this in Construct?

  • $9 a month, no other subscription first. Construct Lite includes 2 agents, 50 steps per task, 3 scheduled tasks, and an agent email address. There is also a 7-day Pro trial.
  • A whole workspace, not only a machine. Each agent works with files, live browser runs, a sandbox terminal, its own email inbox, and apps from a live integration catalog plus your own MCP tools.
  • Work saved as it goes. Finished work lands in workspace files as it is produced, so a run that stops at step 30 still leaves steps 1 to 29 for the next attempt.
  • Schedules that run with every device off. Calendar schedules run on Construct's servers, so the weekly report arrives whether or not your laptop is open.
  • Memory you can read and fix. Open what the agent has learned, correct a fact, or delete it.
  • One workspace for the team, on the model you choose. Team workspaces have Owner, Admin, and Member roles and no member limit. Pro adds your own keys for OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, or xAI.

What is an AI agent with its own computer, exactly?

A chat assistant answers inside a conversation. An agent with its own computer is given somewhere to work: it can open a website, log in, download a file, run a script against it, save the result, and pick the job up tomorrow from what it left behind.

Satya Nadella put the idea in one line on April 22, 2026: "Every agent will need its own computer." He was announcing Microsoft's hosted agents in Foundry, where, in his words, "every agent gets its own dedicated enterprise-grade sandbox, with durable state, built-in identity and governance" (Nadella on X; Microsoft Foundry announcement).

You will see the same thing sold under several names: always-on agent, cloud agent, background agent, AI employee, AI coworker, computer-use agent. The label matters less than four properties:

  1. A machine it controls. A real browser and usually a terminal, not just API calls.
  2. State that persists. Files, logins, and memory survive between tasks.
  3. Work that runs without you. Schedules, triggers, or long jobs that do not need an open tab.
  4. An identity to act with. Your connected accounts, its own inbox, or both.

A product with only the first is a computer-use feature inside a chat. Construct has all four. Our guide to what an AI employee is covers the wider category these products sit in.

Why did every platform ship one in 2026?

Because the model stopped being the bottleneck. Agents could already click and type in 2025. What they lacked was somewhere to stay. A browser that closes when your laptop sleeps cannot run a weekly report, and an agent that loses its files between tasks starts every job from zero.

The launches came in a tight cluster. Every date below is from the vendor or from press coverage we checked on October 1, 2026:

  • February 2026: Perplexity launched Computer, a cloud agent that "runs entirely in the cloud," for Perplexity Max subscribers (TechCrunch).
  • March 12, 2026: Genspark launched Claw, which runs 24/7 on a dedicated cloud computer (Genspark help center; launch date from Sliq).
  • May 19, 2026: Google announced Gemini Spark, a personal agent that keeps working "even when you close your laptop or lock your phone," starting with US Google AI Ultra subscribers (Google). It is still rolling out: Google AI Pro subscribers in India and more than 160 other countries were added from late July (Google India; eWeek).
  • July 7, 2026: Claude Cowork moved sessions to the cloud and onto web and mobile, so tasks keep running with the laptop closed (Automaton Agency; Anthropic's Cowork guide). On September 16, Anthropic merged Cowork into the main Claude interface (TechCrunch).
  • August 11, 2026: xAI introduced Grok Bot, AI teammates that work from a cloud computer while you are away (xAI).
  • September 8, 2026: Meta launched Muse, which runs on "Muse Secure VM," a "dedicated, secure computer with its own browser" (TechCrunch).
  • September 23, 2026: Simular made Sai generally available, running on cloud machines it provisions or on your own device (release coverage).
  • September 28, 2026: Manus 2.0 added an always-on Cloud Computer (Manus).
  • September 29, 2026: OpenAI launched dots, where "each dot has its own cloud computer and browser" (The Next Web). The same day, Meta launched Muse for Small Business (TestingCatalog).

Smaller companies have been building the same thing. Viktor describes its Slack agent as having "his own computer in the cloud where he writes and runs code" (Viktor), and Construct gives each agent a persistent cloud workspace that is not tied to any one model vendor. What changed this summer is that the default assistant on your phone started to come with one.

How does an AI agent with its own computer work?

Strip away the branding and most of these products have the same five parts. Here is what each one looks like in Construct.

1. A sandbox or virtual machine. The agent's actions run in an isolated environment on the vendor's servers. Some vendors keep a whole machine switched on for you (Simular's $500 Sai Unlimited plan includes an "Always-on cloud computer (Windows or Linux)," Sai pricing). Others keep your files and state permanently and start the compute only when there is work, as Microsoft's hosted agents do (Microsoft). Construct takes the second approach: workspace files are permanent, and a Linux sandbox starts when the agent needs one.

2. A browser the agent drives. This is what lets it work in tools that have no integration: a supplier portal, a government form, a dashboard behind a login. Construct runs live browser runs inside the agent's workspace, and what it collects lands in Files.

3. Credentials and app connections. The agent acts through connected accounts (Gmail, Slack, a CRM), through logins saved in its browser, or through an identity of its own. Construct connects apps from a live integration catalog, adds your own MCP tools, and gives every agent its own email address, so it can send as itself instead of as you. This is the part that makes an agent useful and the part that needs the most care.

4. Schedules and triggers. Work starts from a calendar entry, an incoming email, or a message, not only from you typing. In Construct, Calendar schedules run on the server with your laptop closed, and you can hand the agent work from the web, Slack, Telegram, Discord, or by emailing its inbox.

Silent product demo: Construct's Calendar showing scheduled agent jobs and workflow runs. An agent prompt, a connected-app action, or a complete workflow can run once or on a cadence and keeps its result history.

5. Memory and files. What the agent learned and produced is still there for the next run. That is what turns a clever one-off into something you can hand a weekly job. In Construct, you can open that memory, correct a fact, or tell the agent to forget it.

An illustrative example

Illustrative, not a customer case study. A two-person agency wants a Monday briefing on five competitors' pricing pages. On Sunday night the Construct Calendar fires. The agent opens each page in its browser, saves a copy, compares it with last week's saved copy in Files, writes a one-page summary, and emails it to the founders from its own address. Nobody's laptop is on. On Monday the summary, the five snapshots, and an Activity record of what the agent did are sitting in the workspace, and next week's run starts from this week's files.

None of those steps is hard. Each one just needs a place to run and a place to keep things.

Why does it matter?

Three kinds of work become possible that a chat window cannot hold.

Long jobs. A task that takes 40 minutes of browsing and file work does not fit in a request that times out when you switch tabs. On its own machine, the agent can grind through it.

Recurring work. Monthly reports, daily inbox triage, weekly checks. The value of an agent grows when you stop having to start it.

Work you can inspect. Output lands as files, sent messages, and records you can open afterwards, not as a paragraph in a thread you will never scroll back to. When something goes wrong, there is something to look at.

The catch with long and recurring jobs is reliability. Small per-step error rates compound: a 95% reliable agent finishes a 48-step job about 8.5% of the time, which is why agents keep failing halfway through long tasks. A persistent computer does not fix that by itself. It helps only if finished work is saved as it goes, which is how Construct works: a run that stops at step 30 leaves steps 1 to 29 behind, and the next attempt picks up from there.

Read next: Your agent has a half-life

Who offers an AI agent with its own computer?

Construct is our recommendation for founders and small teams, so it leads the table; we build it, and the rest of this page explains why it fits. Prices are USD at monthly billing, checked on October 1, 2026. "Entry price" is the cheapest documented way to get the agent, which is often a bundle, not a standalone product. Usage limits differ widely, so an entry price is not a cost per completed task.

Two things the table hides. First, "its own computer" does not always mean one per agent: Grok Bot's documentation says all of your Bots use the same cloud computer and share its files, its browser, and its app logins (xAI docs). Second, the big-platform agents are mostly consumer products tied to one ecosystem, and most of them require a subscription to that ecosystem before you get the agent at all. For head-to-head detail, see Construct vs ChatGPT Dots, ChatGPT Dots alternatives, Construct vs Grok Bot, and our comparison of AI employee platforms.

How do you evaluate an AI agent with its own computer?

Most launch pages read the same. These questions separate the products quickly, and each one ends with how Construct answers it.

  1. Is the computer always on, or only the state? An always-on machine can host a long-running process. A workspace with on-demand compute is cheaper and fits jobs that start, work, and finish. Construct keeps state permanently and starts compute when there is work.
  2. Does it keep working with every device off? Test it: schedule a job, close everything, and check the result in the morning. Construct's Calendar schedules run on the server.
  3. Whose identity does it act with? Your own Gmail, a scoped connection, or an address of its own? A separate identity limits what a mistake can reach. Every Construct agent has its own email address, and you connect your own accounts only where a job needs them.
  4. What needs your approval? Look for documented rules. Google says Spark asks "before performing high-stakes actions like spending money or sending emails," and Meta says Muse for Small Business "will not publish content, send messages or spend money unless the user authorizes it." In Construct, the agent asks when unsure in chat, and for customer-facing work you ask for drafts and send them yourself.
  5. Can you see what it did? Watching a live browser is good. Files, sent messages, and a step-by-step record you can read afterwards are better. Construct saves output to Files, and Activity records each action with a short reason for a limited window.
  6. What happens when a run fails halfway? Ask whether finished work is saved as it goes, or whether a failure means starting over. In Construct, a run that stops at step 30 keeps steps 1 to 29.
  7. How is it metered, and can you cap it? Credits, tokens, weekly limits, and seats behave differently in a heavy month. Find the spending cap before you schedule anything. Construct plans have a fixed monthly price with published plan limits and no per-message billing, and on Pro your own model keys bill you directly when used.
  8. Are agents isolated from each other? If several agents share one machine and one set of logins, they are not a security boundary.
  9. Where can you reach it? Slack, email, WhatsApp, or only the vendor's app. The best agent is the one your team will actually message. Construct answers on the web, Slack, Telegram, Discord, and its own email inbox.
  10. What happens to its files if you cancel? Find out before the work that matters lives there.

What are the risks?

Giving software a computer and your logins moves risk from "it said something wrong" to "it did something wrong." Three risks matter most.

Credential access. An agent that can send email as you can send the wrong email as you. In February 2026, Summer Yue, Meta's AI alignment director, described an OpenClaw agent that began deleting emails in her real inbox after losing her instruction to wait for approval. She said, "I couldn't stop it from my phone," and "I had to RUN to my Mac mini like I was defusing a bomb" (Business Insider via AOL). That agent ran on her own machine, not a vendor's cloud, but the lesson carries over: scope what the agent can reach and test on data you can afford to lose.

Prompt injection. An agent that reads the web and your inbox will read instructions written by strangers. Simon Willison calls the dangerous combination the "lethal trifecta": "access to your private data," "exposure to untrusted content," and "the ability to externally communicate" (Willison). An agent with its own computer usually has all three by design. Approval rules on sending and spending are the practical defense.

Runaway cost. An agent that works while you sleep can also spend while you sleep. In late September 2026, a developer posted to Hacker News that an OpenAI Codex task had spawned 826 child agents and run up roughly $78,000 in charges (Hacker News). Treat that as a claim, not a confirmed incident: the post was flagged, commenters questioned it, and we found no public response from OpenAI. The failure mode it describes is real either way, which is why the evaluation checklist asks about spending caps.

There is a quieter risk too: work nobody checks. Nine reports produced overnight have not saved you time until someone confirms they are right.

How Construct handles these. The agent works from its own email address, so a mistake lands in its mailbox instead of yours, and only mail from your own account address starts a run, so a stranger's email cannot hand it a job. Memory is open to inspection, so a wrong rule can be corrected rather than guessed at. Each plan has a fixed monthly price with published plan limits. And because every result is a file in the workspace, checking the overnight work means opening it, not scrolling a thread.

Why Construct is our recommendation

We build Construct, so it leads this page; here is why it fits small teams. Construct is an AI employee for solo founders and small teams, and every agent works from a persistent cloud workspace: files, live browser runs, a sandbox terminal, a native agent email address, a calendar of scheduled jobs, and connected apps through a live integration catalog (Gmail, Notion, Linear, GitHub, HubSpot, Airtable, and more) plus custom MCP tools. You can reach it from the web, Slack, Telegram, Discord slash commands, or by emailing its inbox.

Construct's computer is on when there is work. Our engineering write-up, all our agents get computers, we pay for almost none, explains the design. The agent loop lives in a Cloudflare Durable Object that hibernates between events. When the agent needs Linux, a sandbox starts for that command and goes to sleep after about ten minutes idle. Workspace files live in object storage mounted into the sandbox, so they outlive the machine. Nobody pays for an idle box, so an account that is not working costs very little to run.

That design is built for the recurring, cross-app job. Finished work lands in the workspace as it is produced, so the next run picks up from what exists, and memory can be inspected, corrected, or forgotten.

  • Lite ($9): 2 agents, 50 steps per task, 3 scheduled tasks, and an agent email address.
  • Starter ($59): 6x Lite usage, 5 agents, 150 steps per task, and 10 scheduled tasks.
  • Pro ($299): 32x Lite usage, 15 agents, up to 1,000 steps per task, 50 scheduled tasks, and your own keys for OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, and xAI, with a 7-day trial.

See current plans.

Before you start. Each terminal command runs for up to 300 seconds rather than keeping a process alive, so give Construct jobs that start, work, and finish: reports, checks, research, file work. Saved workflows run step by step today, without branching or approval gates, so for anything customer-facing, ask for drafts and send them yourself once you have checked them.

Already using another always-on agent? Add Construct in 15 minutes

You do not have to cancel what you already pay for. Keep your ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini agent for personal follow-ups, and move the one recurring job your team needs to see.

  1. Start on Lite for $9, or take the 7-day Pro trial to test your own model keys and longer runs.
  2. Copy the instructions you gave your current agent into a Construct chat, and move the source files into the workspace.
  3. Connect the apps the job needs from the integration catalog, or add your own MCP tools.
  4. Run it once and check the result in Files.
  5. Put it on the Calendar so it runs every week whether or not anyone is online.

There is no import: what another agent learned about you does not transfer. Write your rules into the first instruction and Construct saves them as memory you can read.

When might another agent still fit?

  • You need a process running continuously, like a game server: an always-on machine such as Manus Cloud Computer or Simular's Sai Unlimited.
  • You need the agent to operate Windows or Mac desktop apps that have no API, which Simular's Sai is built for.
  • You only want a personal assistant inside an app you already pay for, such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini.

For a small team's recurring work across apps, with files, schedules, memory, and a price that starts at $9, Construct is the better fit.

Which should you choose?

Choose Construct. It starts at $9 with nothing else to subscribe to, gives each agent a workspace with files, a browser, a terminal, and its own inbox, runs schedules with every device off, keeps progress when a run stops, and lets you pick the model. If you already pay for one of the big-platform agents, keep it for personal errands and give Construct the work your team depends on.

Give Construct its first job this week: the competitor pricing check, weekly report, or inbox sort that keeps landing on you. Run it on demand a few times, read the files it leaves behind, then put it on the Calendar. Start on Lite at $9, or try Pro free for seven days.

item.title: Clef beat Jev on Jev's home turf
item.description: We ran Cloudflare's Clef and Clef-flash against Jev on five production AI agent decisions: 1,053 calls, accuracy, determinism, drift, cost, and what we are switching.
item.content:encoded:
When Cloudflare released Clef on October 1, its launch post carried a table of ten public benchmarks, seven of them led by a Clef model. The Hacker News thread passed 600 points in a day, and one of the first replies was six words long: "Public benchmarks are easy to cheat" (Traictory, Hacker News).

Fair. So we ran the test nobody could have trained for. Construct's agent has about 40 small decisions written for a decision model, and every one of them was written around Jev: the prompts, the questions, and the thresholds, all built against Jev over the last two weeks. That is Jev's home turf. We pointed the same requests at Clef and Clef-flash without changing a line, and scored all three against labelled cases.

Clef is Cloudflare's open-weight decision model, a drop-in alternative to TypeSafe's Jev. On 117 labelled cases across five of our production decisions, Clef reached the right outcome on 92.3% of calls using thresholds set for Jev, against 88.6% for Jev and 82.1% for Clef-flash. Both Clef models returned the identical probability on every repeated call, and Jev did not.

We build Construct, an AI employee with its own computer. Every number below comes from our own runs on October 4, 2026 (UTC): 117 cases, three calls each, three models, 1,053 calls in the main run, plus about 800 more in follow-up controls. Facts about the models themselves come from Cloudflare's and TypeSafe's documentation, checked the same day. The full method, confidence intervals and per-case results are in the paper: Compatible APIs, Incompatible Thresholds: A Drop-In Replacement Study of Clef and Jev on Decision Specifications from a Production Agent (PDF, 13 pages).

  • Accuracy, drop-in: Clef 92.3%, Jev 88.6%, Clef-flash 82.1%, all on thresholds set for Jev. The gap between Clef and Jev is not statistically significant.
  • Accuracy, own thresholds: Clef 93.2%, Jev 90.9%, Clef-flash 90.6%, with each threshold chosen on held-out cases.
  • Repeatability: Clef and Clef-flash gave the same probability on all 351 calls each. The probability Jev's decisions act on moved by up to 0.10, and 2 cases changed verdict.
  • Code changed to swap models: one string.
  • Failed calls: 0 of 1,053.
  • Cost: $23 per million decisions on Jev, $35 on Clef-flash, $93 on Clef. The main run cost about five cents.

What are Clef and Clef-flash?

Clef and Clef-flash are decision models from Cloudflare: you send a state and a set of typed questions, and they return a probability for each allowed answer instead of generating text. Clef is a 27 billion parameter model built on Qwen3.8, and Clef-flash is a 9 billion parameter model built on Qwen3.5. Both are released under Apache 2.0 with weights on Hugging Face, both run on Workers AI, and both accept the same request format as Jev (Cloudflare).

If decision models are new to you: they are the fast, cheap judgment calls around a language model. Is this the same person? Does this email need a reply? Should this tool call wait for a human? TypeSafe calls the category System One models, after Kahneman's fast, intuitive System 1. Our first post on Jev explains the idea and how we put one inside an AI agent's memory.

Jev, Clef and Clef-flash compared, October 2026

Jev 1.13 Clef Clef-flash
Maker TypeSafe AI Cloudflare Cloudflare
Size Not published 27B parameters 9B parameters
Weights Closed Open, Apache 2.0 Open, Apache 2.0
Question types Choice, Score, Noul Same Same
Input Text and JSON Text, JSON and images Text, JSON and images
Context 64k tokens per request 64k tokens 64k tokens
Price per million input tokens $0.042 $0.24 $0.09
Output tokens Free Free Free
Workers AI model ID typesafe/jev @cf/cloudflare/clef @cf/cloudflare/clef-flash

Two details in that table matter later. Clef reads images, which Jev does not today. And the prices are per input token, so the model that counts fewer tokens for the same request closes some of the gap.

How we benchmarked Clef against Jev

We did not write a new test for Clef. We took five decisions that already exist in Construct's code and ran each one's real request builder and real interpreter, the same functions production calls.

The five production decisions in the benchmark

Decision What it decides Cases Threshold today
Entity match Is this newly mentioned person, project or company one the agent already knows? 30 0.70
Email triage Newsletter, receipt, spam, request, or keep? 15 0.80
Memory extract gate Does this conversation hold anything worth remembering? 24 0.05
Notification priority Does this automation notice deserve a toast, or can it wait? 24 0.85
Tool-call risk Should this tool call wait for the user's go-ahead? 24 0.80

Entity match is live in production. The other four are built and switched off, waiting on shadow data. Their thresholds were set by judgment with Jev in mind and have never been fitted to data, for Jev or anything else.

Swapping the model was the least interesting part of the work. This is the whole change:

// Before
await env.AI.run("typesafe/jev", { state, questions }, options);

// After
await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clef", { state, questions }, options);

Cloudflare says Clef is "fully Jev-API compatible". On our requests that held: Choice, Score and Noul questions, JSON state, and the response shape all worked unchanged, and all 702 Clef calls returned valid answers.

The rest of the method, briefly:

  • Cases: 117, all synthetic, weighted toward the edges of each decision. We drafted and labelled them with an AI assistant (Claude) before any of the three models saw them. No label came from Jev or Clef, and the labels have not yet been independently reviewed by a second person.
  • Runs: each case three times per model, one call at a time, models interleaved so they shared the same network conditions, with the gateway cache skipped.
  • Scoring: a call is correct when the production interpreter reaches the labelled outcome at the production threshold. We also report each model's best threshold, found on the same cases, which flatters all three equally.
  • Route: Cloudflare's REST API through our AI Gateway, from a laptop. Fine for accuracy. Wrong for latency, which gets its own section.

Clef vs Jev accuracy: the results

Overall accuracy across five production decisions, 351 calls per model. Left: the thresholds configured today, set for Jev. Right: each model's own best threshold, found in-sample.

With no retuning at all, Clef had the highest score of the three, and the highest or equal-highest on four of the five decisions, on thresholds that were set for a different model.

Accuracy by decision at the production threshold, with accuracy at each model's own best threshold in brackets

Decision Jev 1.13 Clef Clef-flash
Entity match 72.2% (82.2%) 86.7% (93.3%) 80.0% (86.7%)
Email triage 93.3% (93.3%) 86.7% (93.3%) 73.3% (86.7%)
Memory extract gate 100% (100%) 100% (100%) 95.8% (100%)
Notification priority 95.8% (100%) 100% (100%) 75.0% (100%)
Tool-call risk 87.5% (95.8%) 87.5% (95.8%) 83.3% (100%)
All five 88.6% (93.7%) 92.3% (96.6%) 82.1% (94.9%)

Accuracy per decision at today's thresholds. Jev keeps email triage. Clef takes entity matching and notification priority.

The honest size of this result: Clef leads Jev by 3.7 points on 117 cases, with a 95% interval of -1.1 to +8.8 points. That is not statistically significant, and we would not stretch it into "Clef beats Jev". Three of the entity cases are ones our product resolves in code before any model is asked (identical names, and names that differ only in case). Jev did worst on exactly those, and without them the lead shrinks to 2.0 points (92.1% against 90.1%). What we can say is narrower and more useful. Cloudflare's public numbers predicted Clef would be at least as good as Jev on decision tasks, and on private prompts it had never seen, written for its competitor, it was not measurably worse.

Jev deserves its due here too. It won email triage outright, it never made a wrong merge, and it was perfect on the extract gate. This is a close race between two good models.

Is Clef deterministic?

Yes, on everything we sent it. We called each model three times with the same request for all 117 cases. Clef returned the same probability, to four decimal places, on all 351 calls. So did Clef-flash. To rule out a cache, we sent the same requests again with changes that do not touch the model's input (a unique query string, reformatted JSON, reordered keys): same answers, a cache miss on every response, and a new inference ID each time.

Largest change in probability between three identical calls. Clef and Clef-flash sit at zero on every decision.

The probability each Jev decision acts on moved between identical calls by up to 0.10, and two cases changed verdict from one call to the next. Across every probability Jev returned, the largest move was 0.16, and 100 of the 117 cases came back with at least one number different. TypeSafe describes Jev as returning "similar answers for similar inputs", which is a promise of consistency, not determinism, and a wobble of this size is consistent. But a decision layer acts when a probability crosses a line, so any wobble means a case near the line is decided by which call you happened to make.

Cloudflare's post explains why Clef behaves differently: the decision step is non-autoregressive, with choices derived directly from the model's internal representations and no text sampled along the way. We can confirm the practical result. For anyone who has debugged an agent that did something different the second time, this is the finding that matters most, more than a few points of accuracy.

Jev's scores moved under the same version name

This one surprised us. On September 20 we calibrated our live entity matcher on Jev. Real matches scored 0.71 to 0.82, everything else scored 0.34 or less, and we put the merge threshold at 0.70, in the gap.

Two weeks later we asked the same three calibration probes again.

Jev's probability for the correct match on our three calibration probes: one call on September 20, and the mean of 20 calls on October 4 through Workers AI and on TypeSafe's own API with the version pinned. All were served as jev-1.13.0.

All three now fall under the bar. To be sure this was not a noisy afternoon, we asked each probe 20 more times: none of the 60 calls reached 0.70, and the highest was 0.66. Clef, asked the same 20 times, returned the identical number every time. The served version was jev-1.13.0 both times, so the alarm we built to catch version changes stayed quiet. On this benchmark Jev still never merged two different people, which is the expensive mistake, but it made only 44% of the merges it should have. In production, a missed merge becomes a duplicate.

We do not know why the scores moved. Our first suspect was our own route: we call Jev through Cloudflare's Workers AI, which cannot pin a version. So we repeated everything against TypeSafe's own API with the version pinned to jev-1.13.0. Same result: none of 60 calls reached 0.70, and Jev's answers still varied between identical calls on 104 of 117 cases. The route is not the cause. Three probes are still three probes, and our September baseline is one call each. We are not claiming Jev got worse in general. The lesson is about our own setup: a threshold is only as stable as the model under it, and a version string is not a guarantee. Open weights can change that, if you use them: a model you pin or host yourself cannot move under its thresholds. The hosted Clef alias we tested carries no version either, so we will re-ask these same probes on Clef in two weeks.

Entity matching: where the three models differ most

Entity matching is the decision where a mistake is permanent. A wrong merge fuses two real people in the agent's memory, so precision matters more than recall. AI agent memory covers what that memory holds and how you can correct it.

Entity matching at the production threshold of 0.70: 15 pairs that should merge and 15 that should not.

  • Clef caught the aliases this decision exists for: "Jose Garcia Marquez" against the accented spelling at 0.98, "Stripe, Inc." against "Stripe" at 0.98, "I.B.M." against "IBM" at 0.99. Its one wrong merge was "Acme" into a lone "Acme Corporation" at 0.78, a case reasonable people would argue about.
  • At a 0.80 threshold, Clef made 10 of 15 correct merges and no wrong ones. That is our starting point for shadow mode, not a recommendation: it was picked on these same 30 cases, and "Acme" against "Acme Corporation" sits at 0.78, just under it.
  • Jev is not worse at telling people apart. Drop its threshold to 0.50 and it makes 64% of the correct merges, still with no wrong ones, close to Clef's 67% at 0.80. Its problem at 0.70 is that its scores moved, not that it lost the ability to rank the pairs.
  • Clef-flash is quick to say yes. It matched "Acme Labs Europe" to "Acme Labs" at 0.76 and the bare concept "pricing" to "pricing model" at 0.89. For a merge, that is too eager. For a gate that only skips work, it is fine.
  • All three refused a one-letter surname typo, "Mendelsohn" against "Mendelson". Good. Those can be two people.

Thresholds do not transfer between decision models

If you take one thing from this post into your own migration, take this. A threshold is a property of a model and a prompt together. Move the model and the threshold is wrong, even when the new model is better.

The three models are not far apart in ability. Asked to rank our cases from "should act" to "should not", all three do it well: on the four decisions we could measure this way, the ranking score (AUROC) is 0.93 or higher for every model and a perfect 1.00 on two decisions. What differs is the number each model attaches to the same judgment.

The most accurate threshold per model on two decisions, against the configured threshold

Decision Configured Jev's best Clef's best Clef-flash's best
Tool-call risk 0.80 0.49 0.22 0.31
Notification priority 0.85 0.60 0.85 0.61

Clef-flash shows the effect best. On Jev's thresholds it scored 82.1%. With thresholds chosen for it on held-out cases it scored 90.6%, level with Jev's 90.9% on the same footing, and Clef stayed ahead at 93.2%. The 9B model was never bad at these decisions. It was being read with another model's ruler.

The thresholds in the table were found on the same cases they are scored on, which is why the bracketed figures in the results table (96.6%, 94.9%, 93.7%) run higher than the held-out ones. Treat them as a direction and not as settings. The practical rule is simple: swap the model in shadow, log probabilities for a week, and set the threshold from that.

How fast is Clef? What we could and could not measure

Cloudflare reports a median of 209 ms for Clef and 38.8 ms for Clef-flash, against 524 ms for Jev. We are not going to confirm or dispute those numbers, because our harness was the wrong instrument.

We called all three models through Cloudflare's REST API from a laptop. The fastest call we saw for any model was 340 ms, and for every model the floor sat between 340 and 384 ms. That floor is the path: authentication, the public API, the gateway, and the round trip. You cannot see a 38 ms model through a 340 ms window.

Latency per call through the REST API from a laptop, 351 calls per model. Not a production measurement.

Jev 1.13 Clef Clef-flash
Fastest call 384 ms 352 ms 340 ms
Median 454 ms 654 ms 449 ms
95th percentile 591 ms 1,262 ms 1,024 ms

For transparency, those are the raw numbers. On this path Clef-flash matched Jev at the median, Clef was slower, and both Clef models had longer tails, three days after launch. None of that tells you what a Worker sees when it calls the model through the AI binding, next to the GPU, which is how we call it in production. That measurement is next, and we will publish it here.

What does Clef cost compared with Jev?

Cost per million decisions at list price, using the mean input tokens each model counted for our requests.

Clef's list price is 5.7 times Jev's, which is the first thing the Hacker News thread did arithmetic on. Two things soften that.

First, Clef counted 28% fewer tokens than Jev for the same request: 387 per call against 541. Per decision, the gap is about 4 times, not 5.7.

Second, look at the unit. A million Clef decisions cost $93. All 1,053 calls in this benchmark cost about five cents. An agent that makes a thousand decisions a day spends about nine cents a day on Clef and two on Jev, next to a language model bill many times that. If you run billions of decisions a day, price it carefully, and look at Clef-flash at $35 per million. For everyone else, accuracy and repeatability are worth more than the difference.

Clef vs Jev: which decision model should you use?

Which decision model fits which job, based on our benchmark and each vendor's documentation

If you need Pick Why
The best accuracy without retuning Clef Highest drop-in accuracy on our decisions, 92.3%
The same answer every time Clef or Clef-flash Identical probabilities on every repeated call
To pin a version, self-host, or fine-tune Clef or Clef-flash Open weights under Apache 2.0
To classify images Clef or Clef-flash Both have a vision encoder; Jev is text only
The lowest price per token Jev $0.042 per million input tokens
Zero wrong merges at your current thresholds Jev 100% precision on entity matching, at the cost of recall
A high-volume gate that only skips work Clef-flash, with its own thresholds 90.6% once retuned on held-out cases, at about a third of Clef's price
Anything that merges, deletes or sends Clef, at a high threshold Clef-flash was too eager on lookalike names

The broader field is moving fast. Besides Jev and Clef there are open decision models such as Laya, Kev and OpenDecider, and Cloudflare's own table includes several of them. We have only tested the three in this post.

What we are switching, and why Cloudflare makes it easy

Construct already runs on Cloudflare: Workers, Durable Objects, AI Gateway, and Workers AI for the small models. How our agents get computers we mostly do not pay for describes that stack. So Clef is not a new vendor for us. It is a new model ID on a binding we already call.

  • Entity matching goes to Clef in shadow first, starting at 0.80. Jev keeps deciding while Clef's answers are recorded beside it. The threshold we ship will come from that data, and we switch only if real traffic agrees with this benchmark.
  • Background decisions default to Clef, each with its own threshold measured in shadow.
  • Interactive decisions wait for the latency test. If Clef-flash is as fast from a Worker as Cloudflare reports, it is the natural fit for anything a person is waiting on.
  • Clef-flash stays away from anything that merges or deletes until it has its own thresholds.

There is a quieter benefit. In our Jev post we said that decisions which read your conversations or email "wait for the paperwork", because sending that text to another provider is a privacy decision. A first-party Cloudflare model keeps that text on the platform that already runs the rest of Construct, which removes the main reason most of our decisions are still switched off.

We are also watching Cloudflare's new fine-tuning work, which it calls Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions. Our decision layer already records the label, the probability and what the product did for every decision, with no user text. That is close to the dataset such a system wants.

Read next: We put Jev inside our AI employee

How to try Clef

  • On Workers AI: call @cf/cloudflare/clef or @cf/cloudflare/clef-flash through the AI binding or the REST API. The request is a state plus a map of questions, the same as Jev.
  • Coming from Jev: change the model ID and keep everything else. Then re-measure every threshold.
  • Self-hosted: the weights are at Cloudflare/clef and Cloudflare/clef-flash on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0.
  • Read the probabilities, not the confidence field. It means different things on Clef and Jev, and on Jev it changed meaning between our September and October runs. Read probabilities and both models behave the same.
  • Pace a REST benchmark. Cloudflare's REST API throttled our token at roughly 90 calls a minute. The Workers binding is the route for real traffic.

A minimal request:

curl https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/ai/run \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "model": "@cf/cloudflare/clef",
    "input": {
      "state": { "entity": { "type": "person", "name": "Dr. Priya Shah" } },
      "questions": {
        "match": {
          "type": "choice",
          "instructions": "Which candidate is the same entity?",
          "criteria": {
            "node-priya": "Priya Shah (person)",
            "none": "No candidate is clearly the same entity"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }'

What this benchmark does not show

  • It is small. 117 cases, 15 to 30 per decision. A 3.7 point lead at that size is suggestive.
  • It is synthetic. The cases are written to cover each decision's edges. Production traffic is mostly the easy middle, so real accuracy for all three models is probably higher.
  • The labels are ours, drafted with an AI assistant. No second person has checked them yet. A few are judgment calls, like whether "Acme" should merge into the only "Acme Corporation" in memory. We said no. Dropping the five most arguable ones does not change the order.
  • Thresholds are tuned on small sets. The held-out figures are the fair ones, and they are still noisy at 15 to 30 cases per decision.
  • Latency is unmeasured. See above.
  • One day. Everything ran on October 4, through Cloudflare, with Jev repeated on TypeSafe's own API. Clef was three days old. Jev's scores moved in two weeks. Either could look different next month, which is the argument for running your own cases on a schedule.

The paper has the statistics behind each of these, the five cases no model got right, and every case where any model slipped. The cases, labels and every call are published as JSON beside it: Compatible APIs, Incompatible Thresholds: A Drop-In Replacement Study of Clef and Jev on Decision Specifications from a Production Agent.

Cloudflare published benchmarks, and people on the internet said benchmarks are easy to cheat. The fix for that is boring: write down your own cases, label them, and run every new model through them. Ours took an afternoon and a few cents, and it told us more about our own system than any leaderboard could.

Where Construct fits

Construct is an AI employee with its own computer: a workspace filesystem, long-term memory, a schedule, email, and workflows you can read before you run them. Decision models make the small calls around the edges, such as whether a person your agent just read about is one it already knows. Planning and writing run on general-purpose language models.

Two boundaries, stated plainly. As of this post, Jev still makes the live entity-matching decision and Clef has only run in this benchmark; this page will say when that changes. And the other four decisions in this benchmark are built but switched off in production until shadow data supports them.

If decision models are new to you, start with we put Jev inside our AI employee. For why small, repeatable judgments matter so much in long tasks, read your agent has a half-life. And if the category itself is new, begin with what is an AI employee.

item.title: Zen Mode: some days you just want it done
item.description: Zen Mode is a chat-first way into Construct's AI computer. Ask once, it works in the background, asks when it needs you, and runs on your phone.
item.content:encoded:
Zen Mode is a calmer, chat-first way into Construct Computer, the AI agent with its own cloud computer. You ask in one box. Your agents do the work on their computer in the background, and a single Home screen shows only what needs you, what is running, and what is coming up. The computer itself does not change: the same browser, files, inbox, schedules, and memory are all still there, and Open OS brings back the full desktop, mid-task, whenever you want to watch. Zen Mode also works on your phone, which the desktop never did.

  • What it is: a second way into the same Construct workspace. Not a new version, not a separate plan, not a lite edition.
  • Where it lives: app.construct.computer. From the desktop, click Zen Mode in the menu bar. From Zen Mode, click Open OS to go back. Same account, nothing to migrate.
  • What stays the same: your agents, files, mail, memory, automations, and Activity history.
  • What is new: a Home screen built around what needs you, a layout that fits a phone, and keyboard-first navigation.
  • Watching is on demand: every chat has a computer panel with the live browser, terminal, and files, and you can take control of the browser at any point.
  • Price: included in every Construct plan, from $9/month.

If you saw a "Try V2" button in the Construct menu bar over the last few weeks, this is it, with its real name.

The 40-second Zen Mode film. A cursor labelled Construct works a live desktop on its own, then a click on Zen Mode folds the desktop back, still running, and a calm Home screen takes its place. A weekly competitor brief is requested, scheduled, and approved, and Open OS shows the same computer still working on it.

Why build a calmer way into the same computer?

When we launched Construct, the pitch was a computer you could watch. Your AI got a desktop of its own, with windows, a dock, and a cursor that belonged to it, and you could see every click. People liked that enough to make Construct #1 Product of the Day on Product Hunt. Watching is still the fastest way to trust an agent you have never used before, because nothing is hidden.

Then something predictable happened. Once people trusted it, watching turned into a chore.

Automation researchers saw this coming a long time ago. In Ironies of Automation (1983), Lisanne Bainbridge pointed out that vigilance studies show it is "impossible for even a highly motivated human being to maintain effective visual attention towards a source of information on which very little happens, for more than about half an hour." An agent's desktop is exactly that kind of source. Long stretches of pages loading and text appearing, then one moment that actually needs a person.

If the only way to catch that moment is to watch the whole run, the agent has not taken work off your plate. It has swapped your job for a worse one: monitoring. We wrote about the same trap from the reviewing side in Nobody merges an email.

So we kept the computer and changed what you look at.

Some days you want to watch it work. Some days you just want it done. Zen Mode is for the second kind of day. The desktop is one click away for the first.

What is Zen Mode?

Zen Mode is the task-first shell of Construct Computer. Instead of a desktop full of windows, you get one place to ask and one place to check in, and the agents keep working on their own computer whether you are looking or not.

Zen Mode Home, from the launch film. Everything waiting on you is on the left, everything running is on the right, and Open OS is always in the corner.

Here is what Home shows:

  • The ask box. "What should Construct take off your plate?" Type a request, attach up to 8 files, @-mention files, folders, apps, agents, or teammates, and pick which agent takes it. Starter prompts such as "Research a topic" and "Schedule a daily briefing" are there the first time you open it.
  • Needs you. Everything waiting on a human, in one list: a question an agent asked, an app it needs you to connect, a workflow run that failed, or a billing or usage limit. Each item has one button, such as Answer or View run.
  • Running now. Every live task with an elapsed timer and a Stop button, plus Stop all when several are running.
  • Recent chats and Coming up. Where you left off, and what your schedules will run next.

The sidebar holds the rest of the computer: Agents, Apps, Automations, Files, Mail, Memory, and Activity. Press ⌘K (Ctrl+K on Windows) to search chats, pages, apps, and files, or to hand the query straight to Construct as a new task.

Zen Mode vs the desktop: what changes and what doesn't

Zen Mode compared with the Construct desktop

Feature Zen Mode Desktop (OS)
Built around Tasks and outcomes Windows and apps
First thing you see An ask box and a Home screen of what needs you A menu bar, a dock, and the agent's windows
Watching the agent On demand, in each chat's computer panel Always, the work happens in front of you
Works on a phone Yes No, phones are handed off to Zen Mode
Agents, files, mail, memory, schedules The same ones The same ones
Best for Delegating, then checking in Watching, hands-on work, apps side by side

It is a view, not a version. Both shells use the same account and the same session, so there is nothing to migrate and no setting to flip. That is also why we retired the working name "V2": a new version implies the old one is going away, and the desktop is not going anywhere.

One request, start to finish

Here is the job from the film, step by step: "Research our top 5 competitors and brief me every Monday."

  1. Ask. Type it on Home and send. The task appears in Running now with a timer, and you can close the tab. The work runs on Construct's cloud computer, not in your browser.
  2. It works on its own computer. Construct searches the web, reads pricing pages in its browser, and writes the brief to Files. If you want to look, open the chat's computer panel with ⌘\. Its Progress, Browser, Terminal, and Files tabs follow whatever the agent is using. If a site needs a human, click Take control on the live browser, finish that step, and give control back.
  3. Steer without restarting. While it runs, the ask box reads "Add to the task, Construct will fold it in." Type "include each company's annual discount" and the running task picks it up.
  4. It asks when it needs you. A question arrives as a card with options, and it lands in Needs you with an Answer button. Nothing else interrupts you.
  5. Make it recurring. Put it on a schedule, such as "Weekly on…" Monday at 8:00 in your time zone. You get a preview of the next runs and a rule for when a run is still going ("Skip this run" or "Queue it"). The schedule then appears in Coming up.
  6. Check what it left behind. A brief in Files, a chat you can reopen to see where each line came from, an entry in Activity describing what the agent did and why, and possibly a memory such as "Prefers briefs on Mondays" that you can correct or forget.

Curious what it is doing right now? Click Open OS. The same task is on the full desktop, mid-run.

Open OS, from the launch film: the brief requested in Zen Mode is still being written on the desktop, with the agent's cursor on a pricing page.

Read next: AI Workflow Automation

Calm is not the same as blind

The risk with any "just get it done" interface is that you stop knowing what your agent did. Zen Mode keeps every record the desktop keeps and puts each one a click away.

  • Activity answers "what did my agents do, and why?" Filter by agent, status, and date, and export to CSV or JSON. Activity is kept for 30 days.
  • Memory shows who learned each fact, where it came from, and which agents it applies to. Correct a fact, or forget it; forgotten memories stay in Forgotten so you can restore them. The memory guide covers this in depth.
  • Mail gives the agent an address of its own. When it drafts a reply, you can Send it, Ask for changes, or Discard it.
  • Stop is always close: press Esc or the Stop button in a chat, type /stop, or use Stop all on Home.

One limit to be clear about: Zen Mode does not add an approval step before every action. An agent with access to a tool can use that tool. For anything you cannot take back, such as a payment or a message to a customer, keep review in the instructions and run the job on demand a few times before you schedule it. The interface got calmer. Deciding what to automate is still your call.

Does Zen Mode work on a phone?

Yes. The desktop was built for a large screen, and on a phone it hands you off with a note: "Zen Mode works on this phone. Same computer, same agents." Zen Mode is built to fit. On narrow screens the sidebar becomes a drawer and the ask box docks to the bottom of Home. Open app.construct.computer in your phone's browser and sign in with the same account.

It is the mobile web app, not an App Store app, so there is nothing to install. It is best for the small moments that used to wait until you were back at a desk: answering a question an agent asked while you were out, checking Running now, reviewing a drafted reply, or starting a task from the train and letting the cloud computer do the rest.

For people who live on the keyboard

  • ⌘K searches everything, or asks Construct.
  • G then a letter jumps anywhere: G N new chat, G H Home, G A Agents, G U Automations, G F Files, G M Mail, G R Memory, G V Activity.
  • ⌘\ shows or hides the computer panel in a chat.
  • Esc stops the current run.
  • ? lists every shortcut.
  • In the ask box, /new, /stop, /agents, and /clear do what they say.

Zen Mode also has Groups: one shared conversation with your team and your agents. A lead agent replies by default, and specialist agents answer when you @mention them.

How other AI agents handle "watch it or leave it"

We build Construct. The table below is our editorial comparison of what each product documents about where its agent works and how you check in, as of September 29, 2026. It is not a hands-on benchmark, and prices are the lowest monthly subscription we found that includes each agent.

How AI agents with their own computer show their work, September 2026

Product Where the agent works How you check in Watching and taking over Entry price
Construct Zen Mode Its own persistent cloud computer, with browser, terminal, files, and an inbox Chat, plus Home: Needs you, Running now, Coming up Computer panel in each chat, Take control of the browser, full desktop via Open OS $9/mo (Lite)
Grok Bot A cloud computer per Bot that keeps working 24/7 Conversation; Bots "only come back when something needs your approval" Open Agent Computer shows clicks, typing, and navigation; take control for passwords, 2FA, and payments $20/mo (Cursor Pro)
Claude, with Cowork in the main chat Anthropic's servers, in an isolated environment One chat window that routes each request, since September 16, 2026 Shows what Claude is planning and doing so you can steer $20/mo (Pro)
ChatGPT Work OpenAI's cloud, with a separate cloud browser The conversation; you approve consequential actions Follow progress in the chat; take over its computer on mobile and desktop $20/mo (Plus)
Manus 2.0 A Cloud Computer, or your own computer in an authorized session Chat, plus event-triggered Automations A visible workspace, which you can watch live from your phone $20/mo (Pro)

The pattern is hard to miss: everyone has converged on calm by default, with the computer on demand. When Anthropic merged Cowork into the main Claude chat, TechCrunch reported the reason plainly: "customers often struggled to choose the right tab for the right task." OpenAI removed ChatGPT's standalone agent mode in August 2026 and moved browsing into Work's cloud browser, and a community thread titled "Agent mode was removed with no real replacement" shows how much some people valued seeing the browser.

Where Construct is different:

  • Two full views of one computer. Zen Mode is not a chat with a preview window attached. The complete desktop, with its windowed browser, terminal, editor, and calendar, is one click away and shows the same work.
  • A workspace that outlives the chat. Files, a native agent inbox, memory you can correct, schedules, workflows, and internal apps your agents build all stay in one place for the next job.
  • The lowest entry price here. Construct Lite is $9/month, $11 below the next cheapest option in the table. That compares starting prices, not equal usage, as our Grok Bot comparison explains.

Where another product may fit better: if you already pay for Cursor, SuperGrok, ChatGPT Plus, or Claude Pro, try the agent you already have first. And Construct works on its own cloud computer, not yours. If the job depends on files or apps that only exist on your own machine, a product that can operate your computer, such as Manus in an authorized session, is the more direct fit.

When should you open the desktop instead?

  • You want to watch a long browser job from start to finish, or keep several apps side by side.
  • You want the windowed apps. The standalone browser, terminal, editor, and calendar live on the desktop.
  • You are showing Construct to someone new. Watching an agent use a computer is still the quickest way to understand what it can do.

Switching is one click each way, and nothing you do in one view is lost in the other.

What does Zen Mode cost?

Nothing extra. Zen Mode is part of Construct, and plan limits are the same whichever view you use.

Construct plans, billed monthly

Plan Monthly price Agents Scheduled tasks Steps per task Parallel background jobs
Lite $9 Up to 2 3 Up to 50 2
Starter $59 Up to 5 10 Up to 150 4
Pro $299 Up to 15 50 Up to 1,000 8

Every plan includes an agent email address. Pro adds bring-your-own-key support for supported model providers and has a 7-day trial. Check the current plans before you buy, because prices and limits can change.

Try Zen Mode

If you are new to Construct, sign up and you start in Zen Mode. If you already use the desktop, click Zen Mode in the menu bar, or open app.construct.computer directly.

Then give it the job you usually babysit: the weekly report, the inbox sweep, the research you keep meaning to do. Ask once, close the tab, and come back when it needs you. Your AI keeps its computer. You get your day back.

Sources
